children: Dell says its backlog is 'rigorously vetted for customer quality and access to capital, land and power'
Dell's stock has been one of the hottest in the S&P 500 this year.
Dell Technologies' business has more than doubled within a year's time, reflecting the company's ability to capitalize on fervent artificial-intelligence demand.

The maker of servers, storage products and other equipment just posted $54.9 billion in revenue for its October quarter, up 103% from a year before and well ahead of the FactSet consensus, which was for $49.3 billion.

Dell (DELL) finished out the October quarter with a $132.2 billion AI backlog, a company record, after it booked $60.2 billion in orders. These were "each rigorously vetted for customer quality and access to capital, land and power," Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke said in a statement Tuesday.
"Within the neocloud segment, we remain highly selective about the partners we work with and the end customers supporting their demand," Clarke added in prepared remarks.

Dell also boosted its outlook for the full year on various metrics. For instance, the company now expects $202 billion in revenue for the fiscal year that ends in January, up from a forecast of $192 billion previously.
The company is now targeting 216% growth in revenue from AI-optimized servers, or $78 billion in sales from that category. Dell was previously modeling $74 billion.

Dell topped expectations with its forecast for the January quarter. That calls for $56.3 billion in revenue, up 69% from a year prior, and $8.40 in adjusted earnings per share, up 116%. That compares with the $53.6 billion and $7.49, respectively, that analysts tracked by FactSet had been modeling.

"As AI infrastructure becomes more complex, our competitive advantage strengthened and our momentum accelerates," Clarke said on the earnings call, according to a transcript provided by AlphaSense. He noted the company's "purpose-built bespoke solutions" that are tailored to the needs of different customers.

Shares of Dell have ranked among the S&P 500's SPX best performers for the year, up 135%. Earnings proved a big test in the face of questions about the sustainability of AI demand and the company's links to Nvidia (NVDA). Furthermore, rival HPE (HPE) reported results a day earlier, spooking investors with its profit-margin forecast.
Dell's stock rose about 1% in Tuesday's after-hours action. Shares had fallen about 12% in the regular session, in sympathy with both the reaction to HPE's report and a broader AI selloff.

The margin picture at Dell has been improving. Within the company's infrastructure-solutions group, which includes AI servers, operating margins expanded to 17% from 12.4% a year earlier. Operating margins are a measure of the amount of money a company retains after paying for its operating expenses.
On the earnings call, Clarke noted that the ISG division "drives the vast majority of our growth and profit."

Dell is also demonstrating operating leverage, as revenue grows more quickly than operating expenses. And the company continues to prioritize capital returns, doling out $4.9 billion to shareholders in the forms of dividends and buybacks during the October quarter.
